messages.subject: Impossible posterior samples using custom distribution and sampler
parts:
I'm getting negative values in my posterior samples even though my custom-written sampler is strictly positive. Something is obviously wrong.

The Jeffreys' prior for parameter b ~ sd(1/(b+S)) where sd() is standard deviation and S is a vector of data.

I've been tinkering with my custom distribution 'db' and so I first call:
deregisterDistributions('db')

Since my distribution is a function of data, I just stick those data into the density function as 'Si':

deregisterDistributions('db')
    #BEGIN density function for beta, b
    db<- nimbleFunction(
      run = function(x = double(0), log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
        Si =  c(1978,  2477,  2119, 13707, 13129,  3360,  1995,  8774,  2429,  4906, 16811, 15000, 19250,  1686,  4706, 20550, 1361,  7102)
        returnType(double(0))
        logProb <- log(sd(1/(x+Si))) 
        if(log) return(logProb)
        else return(exp(logProb)) 
      })

I use rejection sampling for the random sampler.  This sure looks like 'b' is strictly positive:
rb<- nimbleFunction(
      run = function(n = integer(0)){
        Si =  c(1978,  2477,  2119, 13707, 13129,  3360,  1995,  8774,  2429,  4906, 16811, 15000, 19250,  1686,  4706, 20550, 1361,  7102)
        
        returnType(double(0))
        if(n != 1) print("rb only allows n = 1; using n = 1.")
        x<-runif(1,0,10000)
        b<-runif(1,0,0.0003)
        while (b > sd(1/(x+Si))){
          x<-runif(1,0,10000)
          b<-runif(1,0,0.0003)
        }
        return(b)
      })
    

Yet when I implement the model...
  BHCode <- nimbleCode({
      for (t in 1:Years) {
        logR[t] ~ dnorm(loga+log(S[t])-log(b+S[t]), sd = sigma) 
      }
      a<-exp(loga)
      loga ~ dunif(0, 20)
      b ~ db()
      sigma<-exp(logsigma)
      logsigma~dunif(-2,2)
    })
    BHConstants <- list(Years=length(S))
    BHData<-list(logR=log(R),S=S)
    BHInits <- list(loga = c(8), b = c(700) ,logsigma = c(0.3))    
    mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = BHCode, constants = BHConstants,
                           data = BHData, inits = BHInits,
                           nchains = 3, niter = 1000000,
                           summary = TRUE, WAIC = FALSE,
                           monitors = c('a','b','sigma'))
...I somehow get a posterior for 'b' with mean = -115. How is my posterior mean negative when my sampler doesn't (shouldn't) propose negative values?

The example should be reproducible if you use...
R = c(2152, 2584, 2381, 1274,  812,  489, 1075, 4042, 4618, 2201, 1042,  896, 6371, 1002, 1016,  593,  450,  818)
...in the 'BHData' line.

All insights appreciated!

-Matt Falcy

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Impossible posterior samples using custom distribution and sampler
parts:
hi Matt,

The 'r' function in a user-defined distribution (or any of the distributions we provide) is NOT used in MCMC sampling (except for the case of a node that has no dependent nodes). Rather, NIMBLE's configureMCMC function assigns samplers to each node. If you use the "printSamplers" method on an MCMC configuration object you can see what samplers are being assigned to the different nodes in the model.  And if your density function is positive for negative values of the random variable, then our samplers will sample negative values during the MCMC.

Another way to put this is that in NIMBLE, the "r" function would sample from the prior, but in MCMC sampling one needs to sample from the posterior (conditional on the current values of the other nodes in the model). 

If you would like to set up a specific sampler that will get used in an MCMC, you'll need to write a user-defined sampler, as discussed in Section 15.5 of the NIMBLE User Manual.

-Chris

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Impossible posterior samples using custom distribution and sampler
parts:
hi Matt,

Ok, glad that some of the issue was just a question of language.

NIMBLE's MCMC uses the "d" function to calculate priors (and likelihoods), so the key is whether the "d" function implements the fact that your prior is strictly positive by assigning 0 density to negative values of the random variable. The "r" function is unused unless a specific algorithm needs to simulate from the prior, which in our built-in MCMC samplers only happens for "predictive" nodes, i.e., those with no dependents. 

-chris
